title: Compress Images Before You Upload: A Faster Website Workflow
author: Jay Barker
summary: You run Lighthouse on a page you just shipped, and there it is again, right at the top of the report: "Properly size images." Underneath, a list of offenders, led by a 4.2 MB hero photo that someone exported straight from a camera and dropped into the CMS. Images are usually the heaviest thing on a web page, and they're often the Largest Contentful Paint element too, which means they directly affect how fast your page feels and how it scores in Core Web Vitals. The fix isn't complicated, but it does need a consistent workflow, because "remember to compress it" is not a process. So if you've been searching for how to compress images for a website properly, this is the workflow I use. It's six steps, a short script that does most of it in one command, and the HTML to serve the results the right way. Disclosure: I work with the team behind SEO Site Checker, whose image compressor I mention below. The rest of the workflow uses open-source tools. The Workflow in 60 Seconds Resize to the largest size you actually display. Choose the right format for the job. Compress with sensible quality settings. Strip metadata you don't need. Automate it, so it happens every time. Serve it properly with , srcset and the right loading hints. Why Compress Before Upload, Not After Most CMS platforms and plugins can optimize images after you upload them. That's better than nothing, but it has real downsides: The original still lands on your server. It gets stored, backed up and sometimes served, depending on how the theme handles image sizes. Big files bloat your Git repo forever. If your images live in the repo, a 6 MB PNG committed once stays in your history permanently, even after you replace it. You give up control. Automatic optimizers apply one-size-fits-all settings. Some are too aggressive and leave visible artifacts. Others barely touch the file. Results are inconsistent. Different people, different tools, different outcomes. Compressing before upload means every image arrives at the right size, in the right format and at the right quality, whether it's going into a CMS, a static site or a Git repo. Step 1: Resize to the Size You Actually Display Resizing is the biggest single win, and it's the step people skip most often. A modern phone photo is often 4,000 pixels wide. If it displays in an 800-pixel column, roughly 96% of those pixels are thrown away by the browser after being downloaded. A few rules of thumb: Export at the width you display, or up to 2x that width for important images on high-density screens. Cap hero images at around 1,600 to 2,000 pixels wide. Larger rarely looks better, but it's always heavier. Generate a few widths (for example 480, 960 and 1600) so the browser can pick the right one with srcset . More on that in Step 6. The reason 2x isn't a free lunch is that file size grows with pixel count, not width. As web.dev's guide to choosing the right image format points out, doubling an image's resolution quadruples its pixels. So use 2x where it matters, not everywhere. With sharp, resizing is one line: import sharp from ' sharp ' ; await sharp ( ' photo.jpg ' ) . rotate () // apply EXIF orientation before metadata is removed . resize ({ width : 1600 , withoutEnlargement : true }) . toFile ( ' photo-1600.jpg ' ); Step 2: Pick the Right Format Format choice matters almost as much as compression settings. Here's the short version: Format Best for Notes JPEG Photos Universal support. The safe fallback. PNG Screenshots, graphics with sharp edges, transparency Lossless, so files are large. Don't use it for photos. WebP Almost everything raster Smaller than JPEG and PNG, supports transparency. AVIF Photos and complex images Often smaller than WebP. Slower to encode. SVG Logos, icons, simple illustrations Vector, so sharp at any size and usually tiny. GIF Nothing, really Use a short video file for animation instead. WebP is the easy default today. Google's WebP documentation reports that lossy WebP images are 25 to 34% smaller than comparable JPEGs at equivalent quality, and lossless WebP images are 26% smaller than PNGs. It's supported in Chrome, Safari, Firefox, Edge and Opera. AVIF can go smaller still, and it's supported by current versions of all the major browsers. The trade-offs are slower encoding and, at very low quality settings, some color shifts. Serving AVIF with a WebP or JPEG fallback (Step 6) gives you the best of both. Step 3: Compress With Sensible Settings First, a quick reality check on the phrase you'll see everywhere: "compress without losing quality." For PNG and lossless WebP, that's literally true. Lossless compression just stores the same pixels more efficiently. For JPEG, lossy WebP and AVIF, compression permanently discards some image data. There is some quality loss. The goal is to make that loss invisible to the human eye while cutting the file size dramatically. That's very achievable with the right settings. Good starting points: JPEG: quality 75 to 85. Use MozJPEG if your tool supports it, as it squeezes out extra savings. WebP: quality 75 to 85. AVIF: around 50 to 65. AVIF's quality scale isn't the same as JPEG's, so a lower number doesn't mean worse-looking. Always compare the result against the original at 100% zoom, especially on faces, text and smooth gradients, which show artifacts first. For tools, pick whatever fits the situation: One-off images: a free online image compressor handles PNG, JPEG and WebP files in a few seconds, with no settings to fiddle with. It's handy when someone sends you a single image and you just need it smaller. Visual comparison: Squoosh, Google's browser-based app, shows the original and compressed versions side by side with a slider, which is great for finding the right quality level. Scripting: command-line tools work well in build scripts: # WebP at quality 80 cwebp -q 80 input.jpg -o output.webp # AVIF at quality 60 avifenc -q 60 input.jpg output.avif # Resize, strip metadata and recompress a JPEG with ImageMagick magick input.jpg -resize 1600x -strip -quality 80 output.jpg One gotcha: recompressing a JPEG that's already been compressed often saves little or nothing, and can even produce a bigger file. If a tool reports zero savings, it's usually because the image was already optimized. Always work from the original where you can. Step 4: Strip Metadata Photos carry metadata, known as EXIF data: camera model, lens settings, timestamps and, very often on phones, GPS coordinates . Publishing a photo taken at someone's home can publish where they live. Stripping metadata removes that risk and shaves off some bytes. Two things to keep in mind. First, keep or convert the color profile, ideally to sRGB, so colors look the same in every browser. Second, apply the EXIF orientation before stripping, or portrait photos can suddenly appear sideways. sharp removes metadata by default, and its .rotate() method (with no arguments) applies the orientation first, which is why it appears in every example here. Step 5: Automate It With a Pre-Upload Script Doing all of this by hand works for one image. For a whole site, put it in a script. Here's the one I use. It takes a folder of original JPEG and PNG files and, for each one, writes several widths in AVIF, WebP and JPEG, with metadata stripped, then prints a before-and-after report. // scripts/optimize-images.mjs // Usage: npm install sharp && node scripts/optimize-images.mjs import sharp from ' sharp ' ; import { readdir , mkdir , stat } from ' node:fs/promises ' ; import path from ' node:path ' ; const SRC = ' images-src ' ; // put your original images here const OUT = ' public/images ' ; // optimized images go here const WIDTHS = [ 480 , 960 , 1600 ]; await mkdir ( OUT , { recursive : true }); const files = ( await readdir ( SRC )). filter (( f ) => / \.( jpe ? g|png ) $/i . test ( f )); for ( const file of files ) { const input = path . join ( SRC , file ); const name = path . parse ( file ). name ; const { size : originalBytes } = await stat ( input ); const { width : originalWidth } = await sharp ( input ). metadata (); // Never upscale: keep only widths the original can support const widths = WIDTHS . filter (( w ) => w <= originalWidth ); if ( widths . length === 0 ) widths . push ( originalWidth ); let largestWebp = 0 ; for ( const width of widths ) { const base = sharp ( input ). rotate (). resize ({ width }); await base . clone (). avif ({ quality : 55 }). toFile ( path . join ( OUT , ` ${ name } - ${ width } .avif` )); const webp = await base . clone (). webp ({ quality : 80 }). toFile ( path . join ( OUT , ` ${ name } - ${ width } .webp` )); await base . clone (). jpeg ({ quality : 80 , mozjpeg : true }). toFile ( path . join ( OUT , ` ${ name } - ${ width } .jpg` )); largestWebp = Math . max ( largestWebp , webp . size ); } const kb = ( bytes ) => ` ${( bytes / 1024 ). toFixed ( 1 )} KB` ; console . log ( ` ${ file } : ${ kb ( originalBytes )} original, largest WebP ${ kb ( largestWebp )} ` ); } Add it to your package.json so anyone on the team can run it: { "scripts" : { "images" : "node scripts/optimize-images.mjs" } } To stop oversized images from sneaking back in, add a size budget check to CI or a pre-commit hook. This one (Node 20 or newer) fails if any image in the output folder is over 300 KB: // scripts/check-image-budget.mjs import { readdir , stat } from ' node:fs/promises ' ; import path from ' node:path ' ; const DIR = ' public/images ' ; const BUDGET_KB = 300 ; let failed = false ; for ( const file of await readdir ( DIR , { recursive : true })) { if ( ! / \.( avif|webp|jpe ? g|png|gif ) $/i . test ( file )) continue ; const { size } = await stat ( path . join ( DIR , file )); if ( size > BUDGET_KB * 1024 ) { console . error ( ` ${ file } is ${ Math . round ( size / 1024 )} KB (budget: ${ BUDGET_KB } KB)` ); failed = true ; } } process . exit ( failed ? 1 : 0 ); The budget number is a guideline, not a law. A full-width hero image might reasonably sit at 200 to 300 KB, while thumbnails should be a fraction of that. Adjust it to your site. The sharp documentation covers every option if you want to tune the output further. Step 6: Serve Images Properly Compression gets you halfway. The other half is making sure the browser downloads the right file at the right time. Here's a hero image using the files the script produced: A few details make a big difference: The browser picks the first format it supports, so list AVIF, then WebP, with JPEG as the fallback in the . srcset and sizes let the browser choose the right width for the screen, so phones don't download desktop-sized images. Always set width and height . The browser uses them to reserve space before the image loads, which prevents layout shift (CLS). Don't lazy-load the hero image. It's usually your LCP element, so it should load immediately, and fetchpriority="high" tells the browser to prioritize it. Do lazy-load images further down the page with loading="lazy" and decoding="async" : Framework and Platform Shortcuts If you're on a modern framework, some of this is built in. Next.js's component and Astro's both resize, convert formats and add srcset automatically. Image CDNs can transform images on the fly through URL parameters. They're great, and you should use them. But it's still worth compressing your source files first. Smaller sources mean a lighter repository, faster builds and less work at request time. A Simple Version for Content Editors Scripts are great for developers, but on most teams, the people uploading images are marketers, writers and clients working in a CMS. If that's your situation, give them a simpler version of the workflow. Here's a checklist you can paste into your team's docs on how to compress images for a website before uploading: Resize first. Crop and resize the image to roughly the width it will appear on the page. For a blog post body, around 1,200 to 1,600 pixels wide is usually plenty. Most laptops have a built-in tool for this, such as Preview on a Mac or Photos on Windows. Compress it. Run it through an online compressor, and check the result looks right before you upload. Use a sensible file name. Rename IMG_4823.jpg to something descriptive, like oak-kitchen-cabinets.jpg . It helps image search and keeps the media library tidy. Write alt text in the CMS. Describe what the image shows, in a short sentence, for people using screen readers. Never upload straight from a phone or camera. Those files are almost always far bigger than a website needs. It takes an extra minute per image, and it prevents the 4 MB hero photo problem entirely. If you can, back it up with the size budget check from Step 5, so anything that slips through gets caught before it goes live. How to Check Your Results After deploying, verify it worked: Lighthouse and PageSpeed Insights flag image problems directly. Look for "Properly size images," "Serve images in next-gen formats" and "Efficiently encode images." The DevTools Network panel shows exactly what's downloaded. Filter by "Img," sort by size and check which format and width each image actually served. A site-wide check catches oversized images on pages you haven't looked at in a while. A quick site-wide SEO audit flags heavy images alongside other performance and SEO issues. Common Mistakes Recompressing the same JPEG over and over instead of working from the original. Lazy-loading the hero image, which delays LCP. Using PNG for photos. Leaving out width and height , which causes layout shift. Shrinking giant images with CSS instead of resizing the file. Serving AVIF or WebP with no fallback for older clients. Exporting every screenshot at full Retina resolution, even thumbnails. FAQs How do I compress images without losing quality? Use lossless compression (PNG or lossless WebP) when the image must be pixel-perfect. For photos, use lossy JPEG, WebP or AVIF at moderate quality settings, around 75 to 85 for JPEG and WebP. Some data is discarded, but at those settings the difference is usually invisible. What is the best image format for websites? For most photos and graphics, WebP is the best all-round choice, with AVIF as an even smaller option where you can provide a fallback. Use SVG for logos and icons, JPEG as a universal fallback, and PNG only when you need lossless quality or transparency. What file size should website images be? There's no single rule, but as a guideline, aim for most content images to be under 100 to 200 KB and large hero images under about 300 KB. Thumbnails should be far smaller. Resizing to the displayed dimensions usually does more than compression alone. What dimensions should images be for a website? Match the largest size the image will actually display, and go up to 2x for important images on high-density screens. For full-width hero images, around 1,600 to 2,000 pixels wide is plenty. Generate several widths and let srcset serve the right one. Does compressing images help SEO? Indirectly, yes. Smaller images make pages load faster, which improves user experience and Core Web Vitals, especially Largest Contentful Paint. Google uses page experience as one of many signals. Descriptive file names and alt text also help your images appear in image search. What's the difference between lossy and lossless compression? Lossless compression stores exactly the same pixels more efficiently, so there's no quality loss, but savings are smaller. Lossy compression permanently discards some data, producing much smaller files. At sensible settings, lossy compression is usually indistinguishable from the original to the human eye. Wrapping Up Resize first, pick the right format, compress with sensible settings, strip the metadata, then serve the result with , srcset and proper loading hints. Put the whole thing in a script and a CI check, and "properly size images" disappears from your Lighthouse reports for good. For anything outside that workflow, there's a collection of other free web tools for quick one-off jobs.

title: PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619): how to check and patch your PHP version
author: Reza Pratama
summary: On 21 Oct 2026 the PHP project shipped fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP engine, known together as PHP2Shell ( php.net ): CVE-2026-109618 , remote code execution via out-of-memory corruption. CVE-2026-109619 , remote code execution via stale global state. Both can allow unauthenticated remote code execution and both are rated CVSS v4.0 9.2 ( CVE-2026-109618 , CVE-2026-109619 ). The flaws are in PHP itself, so updating your framework, theme or plugins does not fix them. As Cloudflare puts it, administrators "need to update the PHP software running their applications" ( Cloudflare ). What's in scope The PHP project says "all PHP installations serving web requests" are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. Wiz says every PHP version released in the last decade, back to 5.4, is affected by at least one of the bugs ( Wiz ). Wiz also says frontier AI models helped its researchers find the bugs and turn them into working exploits. Fixed versions PHP branch Fixed version 8.5 8.5.12 8.4 8.4.27 8.3 8.3.36 8.2 8.2.35 There is no official PHP2Shell release below 8.2; patch via a vendor backport or upgrade. The PHP security team published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 for people who build from source or have no long-term support vendor. Check the runtime that actually serves requests Hosting dashboard or your host. Most panels show the PHP version per site. Ask your host in writing whether the PHP2Shell fix is installed. WordPress: Tools > Site Health > Info > Server. Your own site's response headers. Some servers send X-Powered-By: PHP/8.x.y . Many hide it, and a missing header proves nothing either way. Two catches from Qualys. First, the version that php -v shows on the command line "may belong to a different installation from the one serving web requests". Second, distributions and support vendors that ship their own patched packages may keep an older version number, so check your vendor's advisory rather than the number alone ( Qualys ). Don't leave a phpinfo() page online to check. It shows your server details to anyone. Mitigations are not a fix The PHP project says its temporary mitigations reduce some attack paths but "do not make an installation safe". Cloudflare says its PHP2Shell protections are "deployed automatically on all plans with WAF deployed, including Free users", and still tells customers to patch. A WAF buys time while you update. It doesn't replace the update. Exploitation status Amazon Threat Intelligence saw a PHP2Shell exploit attempt dating to 17 Oct 2026, four days before disclosure, and after the patch said "PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild" ( AWS Security Blog ). CISA's alert the same day said "CISA has not observed exploitation of these vulnerabilities as of the time of publication" ( CISA ). The AWS statement is the more recent picture. AWS also says to start investigations from 17 Oct. On 8.1 or older PHP 8.1 reached end of life on 31 Dec 2025, PHP 8.0 on 26 Nov 2023 and PHP 7.4 on 28 Nov 2022. CISA says organizations that cannot update immediately, or that continue to use PHP 8.1 or earlier, "should take PHP-based systems offline until they can be patched or updated". PHP 8.2 security support ends on 31 Dec 2026, and 8.3 is supported until 31 Dec 2027, so aim for 8.3 or newer if you're upgrading anyway. The 5 steps Find every PHP app and site you run, including staging and anything that bundles PHP (NCSC-NL keeps a list of such products). Check the version of the runtime serving requests, not only the CLI. Update to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or get your host or vendor to confirm a patched build in writing. Firewall on while you patch. Watch. Review from 17 Oct, check Search Console's Security issues report, and rotate passwords, tokens and API keys if anything looks off. Wiz showed the flaws can leak "passwords, tokens, and API keys" from server memory. The SEO part devs tend to skip Does your SEO tool check your PHP version? Search Console only tells you after you're hacked: its Security issues report shows findings once Google determines a site "was hacked, or that it exhibits behavior that could potentially harm a visitor or their computer". Google's hacked site guide names "an older, insecure version of Drupal, Joomla! or WordPress" as a way in, and a hacked site can get a "This site may be hacked" label, drop out of results and out of AI Overviews. I work at Serpair. Our free check checks whether your site advertises a PHP/CMS version affected by PHP2Shell and known CVEs. It's passive and only reads the publicly advertised version, so it sends no attack traffic. "Version hidden / not exposed" is a possible result, and hidden doesn't mean patched. A passive check isn't a full security audit. You get a partial report by work email, then register on Serpair for the full report. Free, no credit card required. Sources and the check are in the original post: PHP2Shell vulnerability: check if your site is affected How did patching go on your stack? Did your distro or host ship a backport, and did php -v match what your web server was actually running?

title: Flutter vs Native App Development for Startups: What Actually Matters?
author: Mister Pulisic
summary: Choosing between Flutter and native development is often presented like a framework debate. It usually is not. For a startup, the more useful question is: Which approach gives this product the best balance of speed, performance, maintainability, team capability, and long-term flexibility? I have seen too many comparisons reduce the decision to: Flutter is cheaper Native is faster Cross-platform is better for startups Native is better for serious products Those statements are too broad to be useful. The right choice depends on the product. Start with the product, not the framework Before comparing Flutter with native development, I would first look at: What does the app actually need to do? How much platform-specific functionality is involved? How complex is the UI? How important is time to market? What kind of performance does the product require? How large is the development team? What happens after the MVP? How likely is the app to depend on device APIs? These questions matter more than framework popularity. A startup with a simple marketplace MVP has very different technical needs from a startup building a camera-heavy application, audio-processing tool, fintech product, or hardware-connected app. Where Flutter becomes attractive Flutter can make a lot of sense when a startup wants to target iOS and Android with a relatively small team. The obvious advantage is shared application code. Instead of maintaining two completely separate UI codebases, a team can build a large part of the product once. That can help with: development speed consistency smaller engineering teams UI iteration shared business logic synchronized feature releases This is especially useful during the MVP stage. When a startup is still validating demand, reducing duplicated development effort can be valuable. But this does not mean Flutter automatically cuts the entire development cost in half. That is one of the most common oversimplifications I see. Cross-platform does not mean zero native work A Flutter application can still require native integration. Examples include: advanced camera functionality Bluetooth health APIs background services payment integrations widgets platform-specific notifications specialized SDKs hardware communication The more deeply a product depends on operating-system-specific behavior, the more likely native code will become part of the project. That is why I would never choose Flutter simply because someone says: ** “You only need one codebase.”** The better question is: How much of this particular product can realistically stay inside that shared codebase? Native development still has clear strengths Native development usually means: Swift or SwiftUI for iOS Kotlin or Jetpack Compose for Android The biggest advantage is direct access to the platform. There is no abstraction layer between the application and many native capabilities. That can be valuable when a product requires: deep hardware integration highly platform-specific interfaces advanced background execution low-level performance optimization immediate access to new operating-system APIs Native development also gives teams more direct control over platform behavior. For some products, that control matters more than the benefit of sharing code. Performance is more nuanced than “native is faster” Technically, native applications have the most direct relationship with the platform. But that does not mean every Flutter application has a meaningful performance disadvantage. For many business applications, marketplaces, booking products, dashboards, internal tools, and consumer apps, the difference may not be noticeable to the user if the application is well built. Performance problems often come from: inefficient network calls poor state management excessive rendering badly optimized images unnecessary background work weak backend architecture Framework choice is only one part of performance. A poorly engineered native application can still perform worse than a well-engineered Flutter application. That is why I prefer evaluating the architecture and engineering quality instead of using framework labels as shortcuts. The team matters more than founders sometimes expect One question I think startups overlook is: Who will actually maintain this product? Suppose a startup already has: an experienced Flutter developer strong Dart knowledge an existing Flutter component library In that case, choosing native development may create unnecessary hiring and operational complexity. The opposite is also true. If a company already has strong iOS and Android engineering teams, switching to Flutter purely because cross-platform sounds cheaper may not produce meaningful savings. Technology decisions should reflect team capability too. MVP speed is important, but so is what happens next Startups understandably care about launching quickly. Flutter can be very attractive here. A shared codebase can help a small team iterate across both platforms without duplicating every feature. But I would also ask: What happens if the MVP succeeds? If the app grows rapidly, does the architecture still make sense? Will the team need more platform-specific functionality? Will the application require features that rely heavily on native APIs? Will future developers be easy to hire? The cheapest MVP architecture is not automatically the cheapest long-term architecture. That distinction matters. Maintenance is where architecture starts to show its value After launch, the product will change. There will be: bug fixes new features OS updates SDK updates analytics changes security patches dependency upgrades A shared codebase can reduce duplicated maintenance work. That is a real advantage. But Flutter applications also depend on plugins, packages, and platform integrations that must remain compatible with both operating systems. If a critical plugin becomes poorly maintained, the development team may need to replace it or write native functionality. Again, this does not make Flutter bad. It simply means maintenance risk should be part of the original technical evaluation. I would look closely at plugin dependency This is one area I think deserves more attention. A startup may initially rely on packages for: maps authentication payments camera access file handling notifications analytics Before using a package for a critical feature, I would check: Is it actively maintained? How frequently is it updated? Does it support current iOS and Android versions? How large is the developer community? Is there a realistic alternative? What happens if the package is abandoned? This kind of dependency review can prevent significant problems later. UI consistency can be a major Flutter advantage Flutter controls much of its own rendering. That gives development teams a high level of consistency across platforms. For startups with heavily customized interfaces, that can be useful. The same design system can often be implemented across iOS and Android without recreating every screen separately. However, consistency is not always the goal. Some products benefit from feeling deeply native on each platform. An iOS user may expect certain navigation patterns, gestures, controls, and system behavior. Android users may expect something different. A good product team should decide whether visual consistency or platform familiarity matters more. When I would seriously consider Flutter From a tech-review perspective, Flutter becomes particularly attractive when: the startup needs iOS and Android from the beginning the product is still validating the market the development team is relatively small the UI is mostly shared across platforms the application does not rely heavily on specialized native functionality faster cross-platform iteration has meaningful business value That is a strong use case. When I would lean toward native I would look more seriously at native development when: the product relies heavily on device hardware performance requirements are unusually demanding platform-specific features are central to the product the UX needs to closely follow each operating system the company already has dedicated iOS and Android expertise long-term platform control matters more than minimizing initial development effort These situations do not automatically require native development, but they strengthen the case. What I would ask a development team If a company recommended Flutter to me, I would ask: Why does Flutter fit this specific product? Which features will require native integrations? Which third-party plugins are critical? What happens if one of those plugins becomes unsupported? How will performance be tested? How will platform-specific bugs be handled? How easy would it be to introduce more native code later? If a company recommended native development, I would ask: Which product requirements justify two platform implementations? How much duplicated work should I expect? Will both platforms launch together? How will feature parity be maintained? What additional team size does this approach require? Could any major functionality reasonably be shared? The point is not to challenge the developers for the sake of it. It is to understand the trade-offs behind the recommendation. The framework rarely decides whether the app succeeds Users usually do not care whether an app was built with: Flutter Swift Kotlin React Native They care whether it: solves their problem loads quickly feels reliable is easy to use does not crash protects their information Framework choice matters because it affects how efficiently the team can achieve those things. But it should remain a technical decision in service of the product. Not the product strategy itself. My view as a tech reviewer I would not recommend Flutter simply because a startup has a limited budget. And I would not recommend native development simply because it provides maximum platform control. I would evaluate: product requirements + team capability + platform dependency + expected growth + maintenance risk Then choose the approach that introduces the least unnecessary complexity. For many startup MVPs, that can absolutely be Flutter. For products with deeper platform-specific requirements, native development can be the more sensible long-term choice. The important part is being able to explain why. Final thought The Flutter vs native debate becomes much easier when you stop asking: “Which technology is better?” and start asking: ** “Which architecture creates the fewest unnecessary constraints for this product?”** That is usually the decision worth making.

title: Two Renames, One Laptop: Goose's New Home and the flisk.sh Cutover
author: flisk
summary: Two projects renamed their front door in the same year, and an agent will follow the old URL of both. Goose's announcement is public and finished. Flisk's is a name split you can see in the install path, the site, and older DEV posts. Treat them as two checklists. Do not merge them into one "migration." Goose: the announcement with a date On 7 April 2026 Michael Neale wrote that Block had donated goose to the Agentic AI Foundation, alongside MCP and AGENTS.md. The operational changes in that post are small: Docs: goose-docs.ai . Old doc links redirect. Bookmarks still need an update. Code: github.com/aaif-goose/goose , including related repos in the aaif-goose org. block/goose redirects, which hides the break until a script clones the old org and fails in CI. Remote: git remote set-url origin git@github.com:aaif-goose/goose.git Everything else in that post: same project, same community, same mission. Still open source. Still the same agent. The foundation itself was announced on 9 December 2025. April is when the repo and docs actually moved. Today's AAIF note (four new projects, 10 total) does not move Goose again. If your Flisk repo has a Goose recipe, the failure looks like this: the recipe curls a block/goose release asset, or a skill links to the old docs path, and the redirect works in a browser but not in the script. Point the recipe at aaif-goose/goose and at goose-docs.ai. Then stop. You do not need a new Flisk stack to finish that rename. flisk.sh: the rename you can see without a press release A Rebranding discussion was opened on 21 October 2026 by odykyi in the flisk-sh announcements category ( discussion 1790 ). I am not going to invent the body of that thread. The public surface is enough to write the cutover, and it disagrees with itself in places. What is consistent: Site and install host: flisk.sh . The headline is flisk up , not a deploy, not a Compose file you maintain. Package people are told to install: @flisk-sh/flisk . Repo people are sent to: github.com/flisk-sh/flisk . Older posts and some README lines still say tdk , tdk up , and tdk-landscape/tdk-cli-core . A 22 October DEV post from the project says the binary on the site today is flisk , and that older posts say tdk . Bind address, if you override it, is still TDK_BIND_ADDRESS . The env name did not get the new brand. What you should verify on the machine, not in a blog: npm install -g @flisk-sh/flisk flisk --version command -v flisk command -v tdk flisk --help | head If npm install -g @flisk-sh/flisk puts tdk on your PATH and not flisk , believe the binary, not this post. A 21 October DEV note already flagged that the README and the site do not say the same thing about the command name. An agent that "fixes" that by rewriting .autogenerated/ will lose the fix on the next generate. The cutover order Do Goose first. It does not touch containers. Update clones, recipes, and doc links to aaif-goose/goose and goose-docs.ai. Confirm goose configure still talks to the provider you pay. The April post did not change providers. Add .gooseignore for .autogenerated/ and .env before you let that agent into a Flisk repo. Then Flisk, on one stack, not the monorepo. flisk doctor flisk up shop --dry-run flisk config verify doctor is the machine. dry-run is the URL list with no containers. config verify is the drift check: generated files must match what the CLI would write. If verify fails, the fix is to regenerate from service.json , not to patch the Dockerfile so the names tdk and flisk both appear. Node.js 22.12 or newer. Docker. Tilt. macOS and Linux start the stack directly. Native Windows can inspect. Starting the stack there needs Ubuntu on WSL2. Those requirements did not change because the banner changed. What an agent should be told, in four lines Goose lives at github.com/aaif-goose/goose. Docs at [ https://goose-docs.ai/ ]( https://goose-docs.ai/ ) . Flisk lives at [ https://flisk.sh/ ]( https://flisk.sh/ ) and github.com/flisk-sh/flisk. Package @flisk-sh/flisk. Run `flisk --help` and use the binary that exists. Do not assume `tdk` and `flisk` are aliases. Never edit `.autogenerated/` . Languages: python, go, rust, node. There is no goose language id. Put that in .goosehints . It is the announcement, compressed into the only behavior that matters on a laptop. What not to announce Do not write that Flisk joined AAIF. No such announcement exists. Do not write that tdk is deleted. Old docs, the bind-address variable, and at least one README sentence still use it. Do not write a migration guide for discussion 1790 until you have read the thread. The link is above. The public install path is the part you can ship today. Goose source: goose has a new home, 7 April 2026 . Flisk surface: flisk.sh , one service.json , discussion 1790 .

title: Diagrid's Goose Announcement Is a Kubernetes Story. flisk.sh Is Not.
author: flisk
summary: Diagrid announced a Catalyst integration for Goose on 22 October 2026. A Goose recipe can commit each step before the next one starts: every LLM call, extension tool call, and sub-recipe. If the process or the node dies, the run resumes at the last committed step instead of replaying completed calls. Catalyst plugs in through Goose's existing extension mechanism. Goose itself does not have to be forked. The same release adds LangChainGo and Mastra. Diagrid says this brings the integration count past 15, across Python, TypeScript, Java, and C#. That is a real announcement. It is also the wrong layer to bolt onto flisk up . Two failure domains Goose + Catalyst flisk.sh What dies A long agent run: minutes, hours, days A local container while you edit code What resumes The recipe, at the last committed step Tilt live-update, or a container restart Where it runs Kubernetes, any cluster Catalyst supports, via Dapr Your laptop. Docker + Tilt. No local cluster What you pay twice if you get this wrong Tokens for repeated LLM calls Nothing. You just rebuild an image What you must not do Treat flisk up as the durability log Put Catalyst inside the generated Dockerfile Yaron Schneider's line in the release is the useful one: Go and TypeScript agents on Kubernetes hit the same failure every long-running process hits. Something breaks, and the work starts over. Flisk's daily loop is the opposite problem. You want the API to restart when you save a file. You do not want a migration, a billing call, or a Goose recipe to restart because Tilt synced a directory. Flisk's own contract is narrow. service.json is the file you own. flisk up <stack> generates Dockerfiles, Traefik routes, and a Tiltfile, then starts that stack. flisk up shop --dry-run prints URLs and starts nothing. Dev ports bind to 127.0.0.1 unless you set TDK_BIND_ADDRESS . Production stays on Helm or whatever you already ship. A warm start of 14 tiny services was reported at 4.6 seconds on a 16 GB M1 after images existed. That number is a laptop boot, not a crash-recovery guarantee. Where people will wire this badly The bad design is one container that is the API, the Goose process, and the migrator. Tilt restarts the container because you changed a handler. Goose starts the recipe again from step 0, because nothing committed the steps. The API's entrypoint runs goose up again because someone thought the database migrator and the AI agent were the same word. GET /health goes green while step 4 of the recipe runs twice. Split them. Process Owner Restart orders-api flisk resource orders-api --type backend --language go Yes, with Tilt Postgres Flisk's local database for that stack With the stack, data in a volume Schema job pressly/goose, one-shot, exits Never, except when you run the job Agent Goose CLI or desktop, on the host or in its own service Catalyst only if this run must survive a node death The agent may call flisk doctor , flisk up shop --dry-run , and curl the health URL Flisk prints. It should not be the process inside the API image. Catalyst's promise is "do not pay for the same tokens twice." That promise is void if Flisk's file watcher kills the process between commits, and it is void if you never turned Catalyst on and assumed Flisk would remember the step. What the release does not give you I am not pasting a Catalyst install. Diagrid says the integration is available through Catalyst, with a write-up at diagrid.io/solutions and docs at docs.diagrid.io . Read those before you add an extension. The release does not say Flisk knows about Catalyst, and Flisk's docs do not list it. Also unchanged today: Goose's repo is still aaif-goose/goose , not a Diagrid repo. Diagrid is an AAIF member. It did not take the project. No Flisk flag starts a durable recipe. LangChainGo support is not flisk resource --language go . The Go provider is a net/http service scaffold. LangChainGo is a library you would put in a service you already own. A boundary that survives both announcements Use Flisk when the question is "how does this service start on my machine." Use Goose when the question is "which commands is an agent allowed to run." Use Catalyst only when the question is "this recipe must survive a dead node, and I am already on Kubernetes." If the recipe's only job is flisk doctor and a health check, you do not need durable execution. You need a short recipe and a human reading the diff. Durable execution is for the run you cannot afford to replay. A laptop Tilt sync is not that run. Source: Diagrid, 22 October 2026 . Flisk behavior: flisk.sh and the 22 October walkthrough flisk.sh is one service.json, then the laptop starts .

title: Today's AAIF Announcement Does Not Add Goose to flisk.sh
author: flisk
summary: On 22 October 2026 the Agentic AI Foundation announced four new hosted projects: Agent Skills from Anthropic, Open Responses from OpenAI, OpenEnv from Hugging Face, and OpenSandbox from Alibaba. AAIF is now at 10 projects in its first year, up from three at launch in December 2025. Goose was not one of the four. It is already on that list, next to MCP, AGENTS.md, A2A, Agent Router, and agentgateway. If you opened the press release hoping flisk resource --language goose would start working, it will not. Flisk scaffolds Python, Go, Rust, and Node. Goose, in this announcement, is the AI agent. What actually changed today Project Who contributed it Layer Agent Skills Anthropic Reusable instructions, scripts, and resources an agent loads on demand Open Responses OpenAI One request/stream schema across model providers OpenEnv Hugging Face Containerized RL environments, MCP plus Gym OpenSandbox Alibaba Sandbox lifecycle API, Docker and Kubernetes runtimes The quote worth keeping is the scope, not the guest list. Manik Surtani, AAIF CTO, said the foundation's job is a neutral place for shared standards, with no single company controlling the outcome. That is governance. It is not a Flisk release. The conference attached to the announcement is AGNTCon + MCPCon North America, 22–23 October 2026, San Jose. Nothing in that release mentions service.json , Tilt, or a laptop stack. The Goose announcement people still mix up with this one Goose's own move was earlier, and it is the one that changes bookmarks. 9 December 2025: Linux Foundation forms AAIF. Founding projects are MCP, goose, and AGENTS.md. Block contributes goose. 7 April 2026: Michael Neale posts that the repo left block/goose for github.com/aaif-goose/goose , and docs moved to goose-docs.ai . Old links redirect. The agent, license, and mission did not change. 22 October 2026: four other projects join the same foundation. Goose stays where it already was. If a recipe, blog, or Flisk AGENTS.md still clones block/goose , update the remote: git remote set-url origin git@github.com:aaif-goose/goose.git That is the whole operational takeaway of the April post. The October post does not give you a second remote to change. What this means next to flisk.sh Flisk is the local runtime. One service.json per service, then flisk up . Docker runs the containers. Tilt watches them. Traefik is the local front door. It is not a deploy tool. Production stays on Helm, or on whatever you already ship. Goose is the process that may run those commands. AAIF hosting it means the agent is under the same neutral roof as MCP and, as of today, Agent Skills. It does not mean Flisk gained a Goose backend, a Goose migrator, or an AAIF sandbox. A practical split: You wanted Use Do not use A local API in the shop stack flisk resource orders-api --type backend --language go --stack shop --yes --language goose An agent that runs flisk doctor and stops Goose CLI, recipe, .gooseignore on .autogenerated/ A hand-edited Dockerfile Portable agent skills Agent Skills, once you have read the spec A fifth tag and a fake Flisk flag A place for the agent to execute code Your existing Flisk container, or OpenSandbox if you adopt that project Pretending Flisk is a sandbox standard Agent Skills is the piece most likely to show up in a Flisk repo later. A skill is a folder of instructions and scripts. A Flisk skill, if you write one, should say: languages are python , go , rust , node ; never edit .autogenerated/ ; flisk config verify after every generate. That is a markdown file you own. AAIF did not publish it for you today. OpenSandbox is the piece most likely to be confused with Flisk. Both can sit on Docker. Flisk's job is "start this product's services on my laptop from service.json ." OpenSandbox's job, in the announcement, is a sandbox protocol for agent execution, eval, and training, with Docker and Kubernetes runtimes. One generates your app's local wiring. The other isolates an agent. Do not merge them because both words appear next to "Docker." What I would not write in the same post That Goose joined AAIF today. It joined at formation, and the repo move finished on 7 April 2026. That Flisk is an AAIF project. It is not. Site: flisk.sh . Package: @flisk-sh/flisk . That Open Responses replaces the model config in goose configure . It is a spec. Your provider key still lives in Goose. Source for the four projects: the Linux Foundation release , 22 October 2026. Source for the repo move: goose has a new home .

title: Your AI Agent Probably Belongs in the Data Pipeline
author: elliot hutchins
summary: There's a question I keep coming back to with AI and data engineering: Do we move the data to the agent, or move the agent to where the data already lives? Because we're starting to put agents everywhere. In the warehouse. On the source databases. Inside BI. Writing transforms. Watching queries. Building DAGs. Debugging pipelines. And if you aren't careful, you end up with five agents, five sets of credentials, five different copies of context and a developer laptop somehow holding the whole thing together. That doesn't feel like where this should end up. Take a boring data stack Nothing exotic. You've got a handful of MSSQL databases. Fivetran moves the data into Snowflake. You've got some DAGs taking it through bronze, silver and gold. Then BI sits on top. Pretty normal. Swap MSSQL for MongoDB, Snowflake for Databricks and Fivetran for Hevo if you want. The names change. The problem really doesn't. Now add agents. Where do they go? The annoying answer is "everywhere" Ask a data engineer where the agent belongs and you're probably going to get the classic answer: "It depends." And, unfortunately, they're right. If you're doing BI, maybe the agent should sit near the warehouse and help users build queries and reports. If you're using it for ETL design, maybe it needs access to your transformation layer, DAGs or SSIS packages. Maybe it's managing transforms directly inside something like Hevo. If it's acting more like a DBA, it probably needs to see query plans, database metrics, indexes and workload history. Maybe another agent is responsible for data quality. Another one owns schema changes. Another handles lineage. There are about a zillion places where an agent can be useful. The interesting problem starts when those agents need each other. Your org chart doesn't care about your pipeline The database team might own the source. Data Engineering owns ingestion and transforms. Analytics owns the models. BI owns what the business actually sees. Dev might own the application producing the data in the first place. Those teams aren't always under the same person. Sometimes they barely talk. The data doesn't care. A bad query in the application can hammer the OLTP database, break an ingestion SLA, delay a transform and leave a dashboard showing garbage. That's one problem. Organizationally, it might belong to four teams. And now we're about to recreate that exact same mess with agents. A DBA agent discovers the issue. A DE agent needs to change something downstream. A dev agent needs to fix the source query. A BI agent needs to know the data is currently questionable. Those agents need shared context around the same goal, even if they have completely different permissions and responsibilities. Otherwise we're right back to using people as the transport layer. So who is actually running these things? You can absolutely give one data engineer a monster setup. Claude Code. Five MCP servers. Snowflake credentials. Access to MSSQL. AWS. Databricks. GitHub. Whatever else you need. Run the whole thing from their laptop. And honestly? It'll probably work. It may even work really well. Right up until you show the architecture diagram to Security. There's also a more practical problem. What happens when something occurs at 2 AM? How do I trigger an agent running on someone's laptop because a CDC event showed up? What happens when a FIFO event needs processing? What if a database crosses a threshold and I want an agent immediately investigating it? You can have the laptop wake up every so often and check something. That's not the same thing. If agents are supposed to become part of the data infrastructure, they need to behave like infrastructure. Stop making the agent come looking for work This is where I think the placement gets more obvious. Put the agents near the tooling that's already moving the data. Your ETL infrastructure already has a huge advantage. It can reach the source. It can reach the destination. It already understands when jobs start and stop. It sees failures. It sees schemas. It sees transforms. It can react to events. And, most importantly, it's already running 24/7. You don't have to give some random new service network access to every database in the company. You don't need a developer's laptop waiting around for something interesting to happen. The infrastructure already exists. Put the agent there. That doesn't mean stuffing your warehouse into an LLM There's another version of this conversation that immediately turns into: "How do we get all our enterprise data into the agent?" I don't think that's usually the right question. Most of the time, don't move the data unless you actually need to. Let the database do database things. If the agent needs to understand a billion-row table, it probably shouldn't pull a billion rows into context. Have it inspect the schema. Look at statistics. Run a query. Sample the data. Ask the warehouse to aggregate it. Use the database as the compute layer it already is. Then give the agent the result it actually needs to make the next decision. That's very different from creating another giant copy of your data just so an LLM can stare at it. Sometimes moving data does make sense There are still cases where moving some of it is useful. Maybe you want an isolated subset of production data for investigation. Maybe the agent needs a smaller analytical working set. Maybe you want to correlate data from several OLTP systems without hammering any of them. Maybe you want cheap local execution for exploration before touching the warehouse. Fine. Move the slice you need. But now that movement should be part of the pipeline too. It should have lineage. Permissions. Retention. A reason for existing. "Claude needed it" probably shouldn't be your entire data governance strategy. The agent belongs in the control plane more than the data plane This is the distinction I think matters. The agent doesn't necessarily need to hold the data. It needs to understand where the data is, how it's moving and what it's allowed to do about it. A pipeline fails. An agent can inspect the source. Check whether the schema changed. Look at the ingestion job. Check the target. Inspect the transform. Figure out what downstream models are affected. Maybe fix the DAG. Maybe create the migration. Maybe tell another agent that the application needs a change instead. That's much closer to a control plane than some giant AI database. And now agent-to-agent communication actually makes sense. The DBA agent doesn't need the BI agent's credentials. The BI agent doesn't need production write access. They need to be able to share enough context to work toward the same result. Same problem. Different domains. Different permissions. This is also where humans should show up less There's no reason a pipeline failure should require three Slack threads before anyone starts fixing it. The agents can do quite a bit before that point. Discover the issue. Figure out where it started. Determine what's affected. Gather the evidence. Hand work to the appropriate domain. Make low-risk changes. Run validation. Then bring a person in when there's actually a decision worth making. Not because an agent needed someone to copy an error message from Snowflake into Jira. We've already got APIs for that. The boring infrastructure matters Once you host agents in the data layer, all the unexciting stuff becomes really important. Network access. SSH tunnels. Private connectivity. Credential scoping. Audit logs. Shared state. Tool permissions. Agent-to-agent messaging. Which agent can change what. Which agent can only inspect it. Which actions require approval. This is the stuff that makes the difference between "I made an AI demo against Snowflake" and actually letting agents participate in your data platform. The LLM is almost the easy part. This is basically where I've landed I don't think there's one database where "the agent" belongs. There are going to be agents across the stack. But I do think there should be a place where those agents run, share context, receive events and interact with the infrastructure without turning every engineer's computer into a tiny integration server. For data, the ETL layer is a pretty damn good place to do it. It already sits between the systems. It already has the connectivity. It already owns workflows. It already reacts to changes. We're just giving it something smarter than another DAG operator. Shameless plug: this is the direction I'm building SchemaBounce around. Transforms and DAG management are in the same environment as the agents. There's managed DuckDB when you actually do want to offload a working subset of OLTP or warehouse data, a SQL workbench, private VPN and SSH connectivity, A2A messaging between agents, and permission boundaries so the DBA agent doesn't automatically get to become the everything agent. Basically, the boring pieces you start needing as soon as you try to take "AI-managed data infrastructure" past a laptop demo. I've seen a lot of tools bolt an agent onto one part of the data stack. Query the warehouse with AI. Generate SQL with AI. Build a DAG with AI. Useful stuff. But that's not really the problem I'm interested in anymore. I want the source database, ingestion layer, transforms, warehouse and BI side to be able to work on the same problem without a human spending their day moving context between them. The data already has a pipeline. Maybe the agents should use it too.
